message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of tasks:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from operating systems to office apps. | Specialized for parallel workloads – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each very powerful, with deep pipelines, complex control logic, large caches, and sophisticated branch prediction. | Many thousands of simpler cores, optimized for throughput rather than latency; each core does less work but many can run simultaneously. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) or reduced instruction set (RISC) with support for branching, exceptions, and a wide range of operations. | Mostly SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) – same operation applied to many data elements at once. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory interface, strong cache coherence across cores. | Smaller per‑core caches, often shared memory pools, high bandwidth memory but less emphasis on cache coherence. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Serial or lightly parallel tasks, heavy branching, I/O bound operations. | Highly parallel tasks like matrix multiplication, image processing, neural network inference/training. |
| **Performance Metrics** | Clock speed (GHz), IPC (instructions per cycle), single‑thread performance. | FLOPS (floating‑point ops per second), memory bandwidth, occupancy. |
| **Energy Efficiency** | Optimized for low power per core, but overall consumption rises quickly with more cores. | Very efficient for throughput‑heavy workloads; can deliver teraflops at relatively modest power budgets. |

In short, CPUs excel at handling diverse, sequential tasks with complex control flow, while GPUs shine when you need to perform the same operation on millions of data points in parallel. That’s why modern systems combine both: the CPU manages the OS and general tasks, and the GPU accelerates compute‑intensive parts like graphics rendering or AI inference.
